--- format: live-html: webr: packages: - survival --- # Kaplan–Meier curves and the log-rank test {#sec-km} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: {.callout-note icon="false"} ## In this chapter **The question.** Did women with advanced lung cancer survive longer than men? **By the end of this chapter you will be able to:** - explain how the **Kaplan–Meier** estimator builds a survival curve, and how it handles censored patients; - fit and plot KM curves in R, and read off median survival and survival at chosen times; - describe the **hazard** in plain words; - compare groups with the **log-rank test**, and follow up three or more groups with adjusted pairwise tests. ::: ## Warm-up: remember Chapter 1? {.unnumbered} Two quick questions to bring back the key ideas from last time. ```{ojs} //| echo: false quiz([ { "q": "A patient was still alive when the study closed, after 3 years of follow-up. How is this recorded?", "options": [ "Event at 3 years", "Censored at 3 years", "Excluded from the analysis", "Recorded as missing" ], "answer": 1, "why": "They were event-free for 3 years, and we don't know what happened after that: time = 3, status = 0 (censored).", "hints": [ "No event happened, so status must be 0.", "", "Excluding them throws away 3 years of event-free follow-up.", "Censored data aren't missing. They tell us the patient survived at least 3 years." ] }, { "q": "Which assumption about censoring do the methods in this book rely on?", "options": [ "There is no censoring", "Censoring is non-informative: censored patients have the same future risk as those still followed", "Censoring only happens at the end of the study", "Each group has the same amount of censoring" ], "answer": 1, "why": "Censoring can happen at any time, and groups can differ in how much there is. What matters is that censoring isn't related to a patient's risk.", "hints": [ "Survival methods exist precisely *because* there is censoring.", "", "Drop-outs during the study are fine, as long as they aren't related to risk.", "Groups can have different amounts of censoring." ] } ]) ``` ## The idea The **survival function** $S(t)$ is the probability of being event-free beyond time $t$. Survival curves always start at $S(0) = 1$ and can only go down. The **Kaplan–Meier (KM) estimator** is named after Edward Kaplan and Paul Meier, who published it in 1958 [@kaplan1958]. Its other name, the *product-limit estimator*, describes how it works: the curve is the **product** of the chances of surviving each step. It splits follow-up into steps at each time an event happens. At each event time $t_j$: - $n_j$ = number **at risk** just before $t_j$. These are people who have not had the event and have not yet been censored. - $d_j$ = number of **events** at $t_j$. - The chance of surviving that step, given you got that far, is $1 - d_j / n_j$. Survival to time $t$ is the product of all the steps so far: $$ \hat S(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{n_j}\right) $$ Censored people **count in the risk set until they are censored**, and then leave quietly. They never count as an event. This is how KM uses the partial information from censored people. ## Interactive app: Kaplan–Meier by hand {#sec-app-km-hand} Type survival times separated by commas, and add `+` to mark a censored time. Edit the data and watch the table and curve update. Try adding a censored time *before* the first event, or a tie (two events at the same time). ```{ojs} //| echo: false import {kmFit, kmMedian, logrank, makeRandom, nAtRisk, quiz} from "./js/survtools.js" ``` ::: {.app} ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof kmText = Inputs.text({label: "Times (+ = censored)", value: "2, 3+, 4, 4, 6+, 7, 9, 11+, 13, 15+", width: 420}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false kmParsed = kmText.split(/[,\s]+/).filter(s => s.length).map(s => ({ time: parseFloat(s), event: s.trim().endsWith("+") ? 0 : 1 })).filter(d => !isNaN(d.time) && d.time >= 0) kmHand = kmFit(kmParsed.map(d => d.time), kmParsed.map(d => d.event)) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false Inputs.table(kmHand.slice(1).map(r => ({ "Time t": r.time, "At risk (n)": r.nrisk, "Events (d)": r.nevent, "Censored": r.ncens, "Step: 1 − d/n": r.nevent ? `1 − ${r.nevent}/${r.nrisk} = ${(1 - r.nevent / r.nrisk).toFixed(3)}` : "1 (no event)", "S(t)": r.surv.toFixed(3) })), {layout: "auto", rows: 20}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false Plot.plot({ height: 300, y: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Survival probability S(t)", grid: true}, x: {label: "Time →"}, marks: [ Plot.line(kmHand, {x: "time", y: "surv", curve: "step-after", strokeWidth: 2.5, stroke: "#0072B2"}), Plot.dot(kmHand.filter(r => r.ncens > 0), {x: "time", y: "surv", symbol: "plus", r: 6, stroke: "#0072B2", strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: "#D55E00", strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeOpacity: 0.6}), Plot.text([`Median = ${isNaN(kmMedian(kmHand)) ? "not reached" : kmMedian(kmHand)}`], {frameAnchor: "top-right", dy: 5, dx: -5, fill: "#D55E00"}) ] }) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Check your understanding - Why doesn't the curve drop at a censored time (`+`)? - After a censored observation, why are the drops at later events *bigger*? - What happens to the median if the last observation is censored and $S(t)$ never goes below 0.5? ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"} ## Answers Using the default data (`2, 3+, 4, 4, 6+, 7, 9, 11+, 13, 15+`): - **No drop at a censored time.** No event happened there. The censored person just leaves the risk set, so $d = 0$ and the step factor is $1 - 0/n = 1$. Look at time 3: $S(t)$ stays at 0.900. - **Bigger drops later.** Each censored person who leaves makes the risk set smaller, so each later death is a larger *fraction* of the people still at risk. The single death at time 2 removes 1/10 of the survival probability (10 at risk). The single death at time 13 removes **half** of it, because only 2 people are left at risk. This is also why the right-hand end of a KM curve is so uncertain. - **Median never reached.** The median is the first time $S(t) \le 0.5$. Here it is 9. If the curve never drops to 0.5, for example because the last observations are censored (try `2, 3+, 4, 6+, 9+, 11+`), the median is **not reached**. R prints `NA`. Don't report the last follow-up time instead. Report "not reached", and give survival at fixed time points or the lower confidence limit for the median if it's available. ::: ## Kaplan–Meier in R `survfit()` fits the KM estimator. `~ 1` means one curve for everyone. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} km_all <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung) km_all ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung) #> #> n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL #> [1,] 228 165 310 285 363 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## How to read this output - **n**: patients (228). **events**: deaths (165). - **median**: the median survival time, 310 days. Half the patients had died by then. - **0.95LCL, 0.95UCL**: the lower and upper limits of the 95% confidence interval for the median (285 to 363 days). ::: `summary()` gives the estimated survival at times you choose. Here we use 180, 365 and 730 days (6 months, 1 year, 2 years): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(km_all, times = c(180, 365, 730)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung) #> #> time n.risk n.event survival std.err lower 95% CI upper 95% CI #> 180 160 63 0.722 0.0298 0.6655 0.783 #> 365 65 58 0.409 0.0358 0.3447 0.486 #> 730 13 38 0.116 0.0283 0.0716 0.187 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## How to read this output One row per chosen time: - **n.risk**: patients still alive and in follow-up at that time. - **n.event**: deaths since the previous time shown. - **survival**: the estimated proportion still alive, $\hat S(t)$. - **lower/upper 95% CI**: its confidence interval. (`std.err` is the standard error, which you rarely need.) ::: So about 41% of patients (95% CI 34%–49%) were still alive at one year. ### Plotting with `ggsurvfit` The **ggsurvfit** package makes good KM plots that work with ggplot2. Use `survfit2()` instead of `survfit()`. It is identical, but it remembers the data and variable labels for plotting. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung) |> ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) + add_confidence_interval() + add_censor_mark(size = 2, alpha = 0.6) + add_quantile(y_value = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") + add_risktable() + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1000, 250)) + labs(x = "Days since enrolment", y = "Overall survival probability") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Overall Kaplan–Meier curve for the lung cancer data.](02-kaplan-meier_files/figure-html/fig-km-overall-1.png){#fig-km-overall fig-align='center' width=770} ::: ::: The **risk table** under the plot shows how many patients are still being followed. Always include it. The right-hand end of a KM curve is usually based on very few people, so read it with caution. ## Comparing groups Put a grouping variable on the right-hand side of the formula: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} km_sex <- survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung) km_sex ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung) #> #> n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL #> sex=Male 138 112 270 212 310 #> sex=Female 90 53 426 348 550 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} km_sex |> ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) + add_confidence_interval() + add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") + add_pvalue(location = "annotation", x = 750) + scale_ggsurvfit() + labs(x = "Days since enrolment") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Kaplan–Meier curves by sex.](02-kaplan-meier_files/figure-html/fig-km-sex-1.png){#fig-km-sex fig-align='center' width=770} ::: ::: The women's curve stays above the men's: at every point in time, a higher proportion of women were still alive. Is that difference bigger than we'd expect by chance? Before answering that, we need one new idea. ### A first look at the hazard {#sec-hazard-intro} So far we've described survival as the **proportion still alive** at each time. Another way to describe it is the **hazard**: *the risk of the event right now, for someone who has survived so far*. ::: {.callout-note} ## The hazard in plain words Imagine 100 patients are still alive at the start of month 6, and 5 of them die during month 6. The hazard in month 6 is roughly **5 per 100 per month**: the death rate among the people still at risk. - The **survival curve** answers: *what proportion are still alive at time t?* - The **hazard** answers: *among those still alive, how fast are the events happening right now?* A **hazard ratio (HR)** compares the hazards of two groups. For example, HR = 0.6 for treatment B vs treatment A means that, at any moment, patients on B are dying at 60% of the rate of patients on A. HR = 1 means no difference. Chapter 3 covers hazards and hazard ratios properly. For now, "hazard ≈ death rate among those still alive" is all you need. ::: ### The log-rank test {#sec-logrank} The **log-rank test** asks whether the survival curves are the same. At every time a death occurs, it compares the number of deaths in each group with the number we'd **expect** if both groups had the same hazard. Then it adds up the differences over all those times. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Call: #> survdiff(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung) #> #> N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V #> sex=Male 138 112 91.6 4.55 10.3 #> sex=Female 90 53 73.4 5.68 10.3 #> #> Chisq= 10.3 on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.001 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## How to read this output - **N**: patients in each group. - **Observed**: deaths that actually happened in each group. - **Expected**: deaths we'd expect in each group if men and women had the same hazard. - `(O-E)^2/E` and `(O-E)^2/V`: intermediate steps in the calculation. You can ignore them. - **Chisq … p**: the test result. This is the line you report. ::: Men had 112 deaths when about 91.6 were expected. Women had 53 when about 73.4 were expected. Men died more often than expected and women less often. The test gives $\chi^2 = 10.3$ on 1 degree of freedom, $p = 0.001$, so there is strong evidence that survival differed by sex. ::: {.callout-warning} ## What the log-rank test can't do - It gives a **p-value only**. It doesn't say *how big* the difference is. For that we need a hazard ratio (Chapter 3). - It works best when one group's hazard is a constant multiple of the other's. If the curves **cross**, it can miss a real difference. - It does **not adjust for other variables**. In observational data, a difference in KM curves may be due to confounding (Chapters 5–7). ::: ### Practice: fill in the blanks *This is a live exercise: edit the code, click **Run Code**, and your answer is checked automatically. See @sec-live-exercises if you haven't used one before.* Do patients aged 70 or over survive less long than younger patients? Replace each `______` with the right code, then click **Run Code**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_km_age'} ```{webr} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_km_age library(survival) lung <- survival::lung lung$status <- lung$status - 1 # recode to 0 = censored, 1 = died ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_km_age' caption='Practice: KM curves by age group'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_km_age #| caption: "Practice: KM curves by age group" # TRUE for patients aged 70 or over lung$old <- lung$age >= ______ # One curve per age group, and the median in each fit <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ ______, data = lung) print(fit) # Survival at 1 year (time is in days) summary(fit, times = ______) # Log-rank test survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ ______, data = lung) ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_km_age"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 1 The new column is called `old`, so that is the grouping variable on the right of each `~`. ::: ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_km_age"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 2 The age cut-off is `70`. Time in `lung` is measured in days, so one year is `365`. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_km_age"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```r lung$old <- lung$age >= 70 fit <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ old, data = lung) print(fit) summary(fit, times = 365) survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ old, data = lung) ``` Median survival was 283 days for patients aged 70 or over (`old=TRUE`) and 340 days for younger patients. At one year, about 30% of the older group and 45% of the younger group were still alive. The difference is just significant: log-rank $\chi^2 = 4.0$ on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.04. ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_km_age' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_km_age #| check: true env <- .envir_result if (is.null(env$lung$old)) { list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning", message = "First create the old column: replace the first blank with the age cut-off.") } else if (!identical(env$lung$old, survival::lung$age >= 70)) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Check the age cut-off: patients aged 70 or over should be TRUE.") } else if (!exists("fit", envir = env, inherits = FALSE) || !identical(names(env$fit$strata), c("old=FALSE", "old=TRUE"))) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "survfit() should give one curve per age group: put old on the right of the ~.") } else if (!grepl("times\\s*=\\s*365", .user_code)) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "One year is 365 days, so use times = 365 in summary().") } else if (!inherits(.result, "survdiff") || !identical(names(.result$n), c("old=FALSE", "old=TRUE"))) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "The last line should be the log-rank test comparing the two age groups: survdiff() with ~ old.") } else { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! Older patients: median 283 days. Younger: 340 days. Log-rank p = 0.04. Now answer: is the difference statistically significant?") } ``` ::: ## Interactive app: two-arm study simulator {#sec-app-km-sim} Here we simulate a two-arm study where we know the truth. The dashed lines are the **true** survival curves. The solid lines are the KM estimates from one simulated sample. Change the sample size and seed to see how much KM curves and log-rank p-values vary from sample to sample. ::: {.app} ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof k2Scen = Inputs.radio(["Default", "Small study (20 per arm)", "Large study (150 per arm)", "No true effect (HR = 1)", "Short follow-up (6 months)", "Heavy drop-out"], {value: "Default", label: "Scenario"}) k2P = ({"Default": {}, "Small study (20 per arm)": {"n": 20}, "Large study (150 per arm)": {"n": 150}, "No true effect (HR = 1)": {"hr": 1}, "Short follow-up (6 months)": {"fu": 6}, "Heavy drop-out": {"drop": 0.08}})[k2Scen] viewof k2 = Inputs.form({ n: Inputs.range([10, 500], {value: k2P.n ?? 60, step: 10, label: "Patients per arm"}), median: Inputs.range([3, 36], {value: k2P.median ?? 12, step: 1, label: "Control median (months)"}), hr: Inputs.range([0.3, 1.5], {value: k2P.hr ?? 0.6, step: 0.05, label: "True hazard ratio (B vs A)"}), fu: Inputs.range([6, 60], {value: k2P.fu ?? 30, step: 6, label: "Max follow-up (months)"}), drop: Inputs.range([0, 0.1], {value: k2P.drop ?? 0.01, step: 0.005, label: "Drop-out rate (per month)"}), seed: Inputs.range([1, 200], {value: k2P.seed ?? 1, step: 1, label: "Random seed (new study)"}), ci: Inputs.toggle({label: "Show 95% CIs", value: k2P.ci ?? true}) }, {template: formGrid}) formGrid = inputs => html`

` ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false k2sim = { const r = makeRandom(k2.seed); const lam0 = Math.LN2 / k2.median; const out = []; for (const [g, lam] of [["A (control)", lam0], ["B (treatment)", lam0 * k2.hr]]) { for (let i = 0; i < k2.n; i++) { const tE = r.exp(lam); const tC = Math.min(k2.fu * (0.5 + 0.5 * r.unif()), k2.drop > 0 ? r.exp(k2.drop) : Infinity); out.push({group: g, g: g.startsWith("B") ? 1 : 0, time: Math.min(tE, tC), event: tE <= tC ? 1 : 0}); } } return out; } k2fits = ["A (control)", "B (treatment)"].flatMap(g => { const d = k2sim.filter(x => x.group === g); return kmFit(d.map(x => x.time), d.map(x => x.event)).map(r => ({...r, group: g})); }) k2true = { const lam0 = Math.LN2 / k2.median, pts = []; for (let t = 0; t <= k2.fu; t += k2.fu / 100) { pts.push({time: t, surv: Math.exp(-lam0 * t), group: "A (control)"}); pts.push({time: t, surv: Math.exp(-lam0 * k2.hr * t), group: "B (treatment)"}); } return pts; } k2lr = logrank(k2sim.map(d => d.time), k2sim.map(d => d.event), k2sim.map(d => d.g)) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false Plot.plot({ height: 340, y: {domain: [0, 1], grid: true, label: "Survival probability"}, x: {label: "Months →", domain: [0, k2.fu]}, color: {legend: true, domain: ["A (control)", "B (treatment)"], range: ["#E69F00", "#0072B2"]}, marks: [ k2.ci ? ` ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Things to try For each one, **predict first**: decide what you expect to see, then pick the scenario and check. Committing to a prediction, even a wrong one, makes the result stick. 1. **Power.** **Predict:** with only 20 patients per arm and a real effect (HR = 0.6), how often will the log-rank test give p < 0.05? *Then* pick **Small study (20 per arm)** and step through several seeds. Compare with **Large study (150 per arm)**. 2. **No effect.** **Predict:** if the treatment does nothing, can the test still give p < 0.05? *Then* pick **No true effect (HR = 1)** and step through seeds. 3. **Censoring.** **Predict:** if follow-up stops at 6 months, what happens to the medians and the p-value? *Then* pick **Short follow-up (6 months)**. 4. **The tail.** **Predict:** with many drop-outs, which part of the curves will be most uncertain? *Then* pick **Heavy drop-out**. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"} ## Answers: what you should see 1. **Power.** With 20 per arm, the true HR of 0.6 gives p < 0.05 in only about **1 seed in 5**. The chance that a study detects a real effect (p < 0.05) is called its **power**. Across 200 simulated studies, the power here was about 20%. A real effect is often missed in a small study. With 150 per arm, power is about **90%**. Notice also how much the 20-per-arm KM curves wander around the dashed true curves. 2. **No effect.** With HR = 1, about **5%** of seeds give p < 0.05. That's exactly what a 5% significance level means: these are false positives. If you click through 20 seeds you'll probably find one or two. 3. **Short follow-up.** With 6 months of follow-up, both medians are "not reached" (the control median is 12 months), there are only a handful of events, and power falls from about 55% to about 22% (at 60 per arm). The number of patients hasn't changed, only the number of **events**. 4. **High drop-out.** The risk table thins out quickly, so the confidence bands balloon at the right of the plot. On average the curves still follow the dashed truth, because random drop-out is *non-informative*. KM handles it correctly, but you get less precision. ::: ## Comparing more than two groups {#sec-pairwise} With three or more groups, `survdiff()` gives an **omnibus** test. Its null hypothesis is that *all* the survival curves are the same, so a small p-value tells you that *at least one* group differs, but not which one. The `lung` data record each patient's **ECOG performance status**, a score of how well they manage daily activities (0 = fully active, higher = more impaired). Only one patient scored 3, so we combine scores of 2 and 3 into "2+": ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lung <- lung |> mutate(ecog = factor(pmin(ph.ecog, 2), levels = 0:2, labels = c("0 (active)", "1", "2+"))) survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung) # medians by group ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung) #> #> 1 observation deleted due to missingness #> n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL #> ecog=0 (active) 63 37 394 348 574 #> ecog=1 113 82 306 268 429 #> ecog=2+ 51 45 183 153 288 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung) |> ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) + add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") + scale_ggsurvfit() + labs(x = "Days since enrolment") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Kaplan–Meier curves by ECOG performance status.](02-kaplan-meier_files/figure-html/fig-km-ecog-1.png){#fig-km-ecog fig-align='center' width=770} ::: ::: Median survival falls from 394 days (ECOG 0) to 306 (ECOG 1) and 183 (ECOG 2+). (One patient has no ECOG score, so they are left out.) The omnibus log-rank test: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Call: #> survdiff(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung) #> #> n=227, 1 observation deleted due to missingness. #> #> N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V #> ecog=0 (active) 63 37 54.2 5.4331 8.2119 #> ecog=1 113 82 83.5 0.0279 0.0573 #> ecog=2+ 51 45 26.3 13.2582 15.9641 #> #> Chisq= 19 on 2 degrees of freedom, p= 8e-05 ``` ::: ::: The omnibus test is clear ($\chi^2 = 19.0$ on 2 degrees of freedom, $p < 0.001$). To find out *which* groups differ, compare each pair of groups. With three groups there are three pairs. Running several tests raises the chance of at least one false positive above 5%, so the p-values are **adjusted** for multiple testing. The **Holm** method is a good default. `pairwise_survdiff()` from the **survminer** package does all of this: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(survminer) pairwise_survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung, p.adjust.method = "holm") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> #> Pairwise comparisons using Log-Rank test #> #> data: lung and ecog #> #> 0 (active) 1 #> 1 0.0630 - #> 2+ 9e-05 0.0052 #> #> P value adjustment method: holm ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## How to read this output Each number is the Holm-adjusted p-value for one pair of groups. Find a row and a column, e.g. *2+* (row) vs *0 (active)* (column), adjusted p = 0.00009. **Always set `p.adjust.method`.** If you leave it out, `pairwise_survdiff()` uses a less strict adjustment (Benjamini–Hochberg), and you'll get smaller p-values than these. ::: Patients with ECOG 2+ had worse survival than both ECOG 0 (adjusted p < 0.001) and ECOG 1 (adjusted p = 0.005). The difference between ECOG 0 and 1 is not significant after adjustment (p = 0.06). To report *how big* the differences between groups are (hazard ratios), or to test for a steady trend across ordered groups like these, you need a Cox model. See @sec-cox-groups in the next chapter. :::: {.optional} ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"} ## Going further (optional): what `pairwise_survdiff()` does, and Holm vs BH For each pair of groups, `pairwise_survdiff()` keeps only the patients in those two groups and runs an ordinary two-group `survdiff()`. Then it adjusts the p-values. The short function below does the same thing step by step. It's in [`pairwise_logrank.R`](R/pairwise_logrank.R){download="pairwise_logrank.R"} if you want it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Copyright (c) 2026 Tom Goodale. SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT # pairwise_logrank() --------------------------------------------------------- # # Follow-up comparisons after an omnibus log-rank test with 3+ groups. # Runs a two-group log-rank test (survdiff) for every pair of groups, using # only the patients in those two groups, and adjusts the p-values for # multiple testing (Holm by default; see ?p.adjust for other methods). # # formula : Surv(time, status) ~ group (one grouping variable) # data : a data frame # # Returns one row per pair: the two groups, n, chi-square, raw p, adjusted p. pairwise_logrank <- function(formula, data, p.adjust.method = "holm") { grp <- all.vars(formula)[length(all.vars(formula))] # the grouping variable levs <- levels(factor(data[[grp]])) pairs <- combn(levs, 2, simplify = FALSE) res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(pairs, function(pr) { sub <- data[!is.na(data[[grp]]) & data[[grp]] %in% pr, ] sub[[grp]] <- droplevels(factor(sub[[grp]])) lr <- survival::survdiff(formula, data = sub) data.frame(group1 = pr[1], group2 = pr[2], n = sum(lr$n), chisq = lr$chisq, p = pchisq(lr$chisq, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)) })) res$p_adj <- p.adjust(res$p, method = p.adjust.method) res } ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pairwise_logrank(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> group1 group2 n chisq p p_adj #> 1 0 (active) 1 176 3.456831 6.299095e-02 6.299095e-02 #> 2 0 (active) 2+ 114 17.418509 2.998914e-05 8.996742e-05 #> 3 1 2+ 164 9.084970 2.577187e-03 5.154373e-03 ``` ::: ::: The `p_adj` column matches `pairwise_survdiff()`. - **Holm** (and Bonferroni) control the *family-wise error rate*: the chance of making *any* false-positive claim. Holm is always at least as powerful as Bonferroni. - **Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)** controls the *false discovery rate*: the expected proportion of false positives among the comparisons you call significant. It's less strict, so its adjusted p-values are smaller. ::: :::: **Good practice.** Plan your comparisons before you see the data: you often don't need every pair. ("Each dose vs placebo" is 3 comparisons for 4 groups, not 6.) Say which adjustment you used, and report survival estimates such as medians for each group, not just p-values. A methods sentence might read: *"Survival was compared between ECOG groups using the log-rank test, followed by pairwise log-rank tests with Holm's correction, using the survival [@survival-package] and survminer [@survminer] packages in R."* The references come from `citation("survival")` and `citation("survminer")`. ## Reporting Kaplan–Meier results {#sec-km-reporting} A good KM summary normally includes: - the plot, **with a risk table** and censoring marks; - the number of events and number at risk in each group; - median survival with a 95% CI (or "not reached"); - survival at clinically meaningful times (e.g. 1-year survival) with CIs; - the log-rank p-value, *and* an effect size such as a hazard ratio from a Cox model (Chapter 3). ### Writing it up A sentence template you can adapt: > Median survival was **[X]** days (95% CI **[a]** to **[b]**) in **[group 1]** > and **[Y]** days (95% CI **[c]** to **[d]**) in **[group 2]**. At > **[time]**, **[p1]**% (95% CI …) of **[group 1]** and **[p2]**% (95% CI …) > of **[group 2]** were still alive. Survival differed between the groups > (log-rank test, $\chi^2$ = **[value]**, **[df]** df, p = **[value]**). Filled in for the `lung` data: > Median survival was 426 days (95% CI 348 to 550) in women and 270 days > (95% CI 212 to 310) in men. At one year, 53% (95% CI 42% to 66%) of women > and 34% (95% CI 26% to 43%) of men were still alive. Survival differed > between the sexes (log-rank test, $\chi^2$ = 10.3, 1 df, p = 0.001). The **gtsummary** package's `tbl_survfit()` can produce these numbers as a table. ## Quick quiz {.unnumbered} Choose an answer to each question. Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons (last line) ``` ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_veteran"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 1 These are the same functions used for ECOG in @sec-pairwise: `survdiff()`, then `pairwise_survdiff()`. Use `data = veteran` and `~ celltype`. ::: ::: ::: {.hint exercise="ex_veteran"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint 2 ```r pairwise_survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran, p.adjust.method = ______) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_veteran"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```r survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran) pairwise_survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran, p.adjust.method = "holm") ``` The omnibus test has 3 degrees of freedom (4 groups − 1). Its null hypothesis is that all four curves are identical, and it is clearly rejected ($\chi^2 = 25.4$, $p < 0.001$). The pairwise tests show two clusters: squamous and large cell have similar survival (adjusted p = 0.73), as do small cell and adeno (adjusted p = 0.76). Every comparison *between* the clusters is significant. ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_veteran' check='true'} ```{webr} #| exercise: ex_veteran #| check: true code_lines <- strsplit(.user_code, "\n")[[1]] # an omnibus survdiff() call on celltype (not pairwise_survdiff) has_omnibus <- any(grepl("(^|[^_A-Za-z.])survdiff\\s*\\(", code_lines) & grepl("celltype", code_lines)) if (!has_omnibus) { list(correct = FALSE, type = "warning", message = "Include the omnibus log-rank test: survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran).") } else if (!inherits(.result, "pairwise.htest")) { list(correct = FALSE, message = "Make the last line the pairwise comparisons, using pairwise_survdiff().") } else if (!identical(.result$p.adjust.method, "holm")) { list(correct = FALSE, message = paste0("Nearly there. Your pairwise tests used the ", .result$p.adjust.method, " adjustment. Set p.adjust.method = \"holm\".")) } else { list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! Squamous and large cell are similar (adjusted p = 0.73), as are small cell and adeno (0.76). Every comparison between these two clusters is significant.") } ``` ::: ## Summary ::: {.callout-important icon="false"} ## Key points - The **KM estimator** multiplies together the chances of surviving each event time: $1 - d/n$. A censored patient leaves the risk set without causing a drop. - Report KM curves **with a risk table**, plus median survival (or 'not reached') and survival at chosen times, each with a 95% CI. - The **hazard** is the event rate among people still at risk. A **hazard ratio** compares two groups' hazards. - The **log-rank test** checks whether survival curves differ. It gives only a p-value, works best when the hazard ratio is constant, and doesn't adjust for other variables. - With three or more groups, follow a significant omnibus test with **pairwise tests adjusted for multiple testing** (e.g. Holm). Always set `p.adjust.method`. ::: **Answering the question.** Yes. Median survival was 426 days for women and 270 days for men. One year after enrolment, about 53% of women and 34% of men were still alive. The log-rank test gave p = 0.001. How *much* lower women's risk was, and whether that holds after accounting for age and fitness, is the next chapter's question. ## Further reading All of these are free to read online unless marked otherwise.
